title: Man. Post. Cap. II §III: Garissoles — fourfold needless; only actualis transgressio meant
pass_a_gloss: GAR. I observe next, that by no necessity, or great utility, the Learned Man was compelled so anxiously and scrupulously to distinguish the subject into four significations; since whoever hitherto have spoken of the imputation of the first sin, have understood nothing else by that name, as can sufficiently appear from their writings, than that actual transgression of the first man himself, by which he violated God's command concerning not tasting the fruit of the forbidden tree. Why then was it needful through laborious windings to lead the reader's mind around, and to make words about sin inhering in us, or our original corruption, and about imputation and the penalty following the guilt itself, concerning which it is sufficiently known that they are by no means treated in this disputation? For it is not asked whether corruption is implanted in us all, on account of which God may deservedly exact penalties from us, or impute it to us, which no one of the Evangelicals ever called back into doubt: That one thing it is delightful to certain ones to call today into Question, whether from that first actual sin of Adam some guilt, and some worthiness of penalty, lies upon the posterity.
pass_b_english: Garissoles. Next I notice that no necessity, and no great usefulness, drove the learned man to divide the subject so anxiously and scrupulously into four senses. Everyone who has spoken until now of the imputation of the first sin has meant by that name, as their writings sufficiently show, only that actual transgression of the first man by which he broke God's command not to taste the fruit of the forbidden tree. Why then lead the reader through laborious windings, and speak of sin inhering in us—or our original corruption—and of imputation and the penalty that follows guilt, matters everyone knows are not at issue in this dispute? The question is not whether corruption is planted in us all, for which God may justly exact penalties from us or impute it to us—no Evangelical ever called that back into doubt. What some today delight to bring into question is only this: whether from Adam's first actual sin some guilt and some liability to penalty rests on the posterity.
source_text: GAR. Observo deinde, nulla necessitate, vel magna utilitate, compulsum Virum Doctum, ut ita anxie et scrupulose subjectum in quatuor significata distingueret; cum quicunque hactenus de primi peccati imputatione locuti sunt, nihil aliud eo nomine intellexerint, ut ex ipsorum scriptis satis patere potest, quam ipsius primi hominis actualem illam transgressionem, qua Dei mandatum de non gustando fructu arboris interdictae violavit. Ut quid igitur opus erat per operosas ambages lectoris animum circumducere, et de peccato in nobis inhaerente, sive corruptione nostra originali, deque imputatione ac poena reatum ipsam consequente verba facere, de quibus in hac disputatione nequaquam agi satis notum est? Non enim quaeritur, utrum nobis omnibus insita sit corruptio, propter quam Deus poenas a nobis exigere merito possit, aut eam nobis imputare, quod nemo Evangelicorum unquam revocavit in dubium: Illud unum in Quaestionem hodie vocari quibusdam volupe est, utrum ex primo illo actuali Adae peccato aliquis reatus, et aliqua poenae dignitas posteris incumbat.

choices.choice: Fourfold distinction needless; first sin = actualis transgressio alone

notes: Cap. II §III Garissoles densify section 166 from locked 1661 Latin (pp. 165 tip–170 tip).
